title: Liquids when the prescription is in g or micrograms and the label in mg
blurb: Convert a g or microgram prescription to match a mg label, then calculate the liquid volume without a thousandfold error.
question: A child is prescribed 0.5 g of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given?

teach.body: Formal rule: before using volume = (want ÷ have) × stock volume, express want and have in the same unit. Plain English: a prescription in g or micrograms cannot be divided by a label in mg. Change one of them, usually to the smaller unit, then carry on as a normal liquid calculation. Part A items deliberately mix these units.

head: Prescription
× or ÷
Matches label in mg
teach.caption: Or convert the label instead: 0.05 mg/mL = 50 micrograms/mL. Either way, units must match.

teach.h: Worked example: Leo on a children's ward
teach.body: Leo, 6, is prescribed 0.5 g of a medicine; the suspension is 250 mg/5 mL. Convert: 0.5 g = 500 mg. Volume = 500 ÷ 250 × 5 = 2 × 5 = 10 mL. Sense-check: 500 mg is twice the 250 mg in 5 mL, so twice 5 mL. Type 10 mL.

teach.text: mg versus micrograms (or g versus mg) is a ×1000 step. Skipping the conversion, or moving the point the wrong number of places, gives a volume 10, 100 or 1000 times wrong. A volume like 0.01 mL or 100 mL for an oral dose is a red flag.

items.label: typical range for one oral dose
error from a missed mg/micrograms step

teach.body: On the note board write "0.5 g = 500 mg" before you touch the calculator. It takes three seconds and catches most thousandfold errors. Round only the final volume, to the decimal places in the stem, and type it with mL.

items: Match the prescription's unit to the label's unit first.
Then volume = want ÷ have × stock volume.
Implausible volumes (0.01 mL, 100 mL) signal a conversion slip.
Round once at the end; type number and mL.

summary: You can now convert a prescription in g or micrograms to match a mg label and calculate the oral liquid volume. You can also spot a thousandfold error from an implausible volume.

A.q: A person is prescribed 1 g of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: No conversion: dividing g by mg gives 0.02 mL.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: 1 g was taken as 10000 mg, a tenfold slip.

A.q: A child is prescribed amoxicillin 0.25 g. The oral suspension is labelled 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.1: 0.25 g was taken as 2500 mg, giving 100 mL.
whyNot.2: 0.25 g was taken as 25 mg, giving 1 mL.

A.q: A person is prescribed digoxin 125 micrograms. The oral solution is labelled 0.05 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: Convert the label: 0.05 mg = 50 micrograms per mL. Volume = 125 ÷ 50 = 2.5 mL.

whyNot.1: No conversion: micrograms divided by mg gives 2500.
whyNot.2: 0.05 mg was taken as 5 micrograms, giving 25 mL.

B.q: A service user is prescribed haloperidol 500 micrograms. The oral solution is labelled 2 mg/mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: No conversion: micrograms divided by mg gives 250.
whyNot.1: 500 micrograms was taken as 5 mg, a tenfold slip.

B.q: A child is prescribed paracetamol 0.24 g. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: 0.24 g was taken as 2400 mg, giving 100 mL.
whyNot.3: 0.24 g was taken as 24 mg, giving 1 mL.

B.q: A person is prescribed 1.5 g of a medicine. The oral suspension is labelled 500 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.1: 1.5 g was taken as 15000 mg, giving 150 mL.
whyNot.2: 1.5 g was taken as 150 mg, giving 1.5 mL.

C.q: A child is prescribed 1.2 g of a medicine a day in four equal doses. The oral suspension is labelled 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: 1.2 g = 1200 mg a day. One dose = 1200 ÷ 4 = 300 mg. Volume = 300 ÷ 125 × 5 = 12 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the daily volume, not each dose.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Divided into three doses instead of four.

C.q: A person is prescribed 375 micrograms of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 1 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
C.why: Convert: 375 micrograms = 0.375 mg. Volume = 0.375 ÷ 1 × 5 = 1.875, which is 1.88 mL to two decimal places.

whyNot.0: No conversion: micrograms treated as mg, giving 1875 mL.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.

C.q: A service user is prescribed 2.5 mg of a medicine. The oral solution is labelled 500 micrograms/5 mL. What volume should be given? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.2: 2.5 mg was taken as 25000 micrograms, giving 250 mL.
whyNot.3: No conversion: mg divided by micrograms gives 0.03 mL.

reteach.title: Make the units match
reteach.question: A prescription is in g and the label is in mg. What is the first step?

blocks.body: Multiply the grams by 1000 to get mg. 0.2 g becomes 200 mg. Only then divide by the label strength and multiply by the stock volume.

blocks.text: 0.2 ÷ 100 × 5 = 0.01 mL: the result of dividing grams by milligrams. It is a thousand times too small.

whyNot.1: No conversion: g divided by mg gives 0.01 mL.
whyNot.2: 0.2 g was taken as 2000 mg, giving 100 mL.
